transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-14
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Park (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (CTO - Orion), Lina Rodriguez (ML Infra Lead), Jamal Price (SRE)

Summary (auto): Deep technical dive on GPU runtime profiling. Focus on kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM performance, CUDA graphs for warm and cold paths, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, and quantization tradeoffs. Action items include sharing benchmark artifacts and arranging staging runs.

Topics:
- Kernel selection heuristics and observed regressions
- TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) vs vLLM per-token latency and throughput
- CUDA Graphs: warmup, static graph capture, and dynamic shapes
- KV cache and prefix caching strategies for conversational workloads
- Batching: dynamic batching, continuous batching, tail latency impacts
- Quantization: 4-bit/8-bit impacts and quality regressions
- VPC/on-prem constraints and secure profiling

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh, happy valentines day, i guess. um quick intros, i'm samir patel, ae on the redwood infra team, elena will go deep on the profiling.
[00:10] Elena: hi all, elena park, se. i'll drive the profile section. michael, lina, jamal, thanks for carving out the time.
[00:18] Michael: yeah thanks, excited. we want to understand where the perf wins are, and whether we should move to dedicated or keep hosted for now.
[00:26] Lina: and specifically kernel selection - we've seen weird perf cliffs on long context runs, so curious about that.
[00:31] Jamal: also need to confirm we can run profiling safely inside our VPC, we can't send traces outside.
[00:36] Samir: yeah totally, we'll cover on-prem / vpc steps. quick agenda, elena?
[00:41] Elena: plan: walk through our CUDA graph capture of a 70-token context, then kernel selection decisions we make at compile time, compare a few runs of TRT-LLM vs vllm, and talk about kv cache and batching heuristics.
[00:50] Michael: sounds good.

[00:55] [01:15] Elena: okay starting with CUDA graphs - so we capture two flows: static capture for the steady-state decode path and a separate path for cold-start where we can't reuse the graph because of dynamic shape or new EOS tokens, etc. the key is minimizing graph re-capture during generation. if we re-capture often you get big spikes.
[01:36] Michael: and your capture frequency is based on sequence length and attention pattern?
[01:40] Elena: yep. we use heuristics: typical reasoning workloads have consistent seq-len distributions so we pin the graph for the common bucket. for outliers we fall back to non-graph path to avoid incorrect kernels. sometimes the parser mislabels model variants and you get a re-capture loop, which is, uh, annoying.

[01:58] [02:15] Jamal: for our tests we saw a jump at token 64 to 65, latency doubled. any ideas?
[02:21] Elena: that often is a kernel-selection boundary - many kernels are optimized for power-of-two block sizes or specific fused attention tiling. crossing 64->65 may flip to a different kernel or switch from 2D tiling to 3D. also padding and kv cache alignment matter.
[02:38] Lina: is that a quantization thing? we ran 4-bit and saw more instability around that boundary.
[02:44] Elena: quantization can exacerbate it. lower-bit kernels may have different tile sizes. also the inference engine (trt-llm) might pick different GEMM kernels when inputs look quantized. vLLM tends to be more consistent but sometimes slower for small batch sizes.

[03:05] [03:30] Samir: maybe useful to show the benchmark table - elena you have the numbers?
[03:34] Elena: yeah. so quick numbers from our internal benchmark on A100 40GB: 1) TRT-LLM FP16 steady-state throughput: ~280 tokens/s with batch=8, latency ~18ms per token at seq=512; 2) vLLM FP16: ~210 tokens/s batch=8, latency ~24ms; 3) TRT-LLM with CUDA graphs enabled reduced CPU overhead and improved tail latency by ~20% but only once warm.
[03:58] Michael: warm meaning KV cache warmed?
[04:01] Elena: warm meaning graph captured and kernels resident. kv cache warm reduces repeated attention recompute for prefixes.

[04:10] [04:30] Jamal: how reproducible are those numbers on our infra - we run on GCP T4s currently and plan to move to Ampere.
[04:37] Elena: T4s will be lower, and TensorRT benefits more on Ampere/RTX-class due to faster Tensor Cores. our numbers are on A100 but the pr axi though, um, practice scales. two caveats: model compilation time for TRT-LLM can be significant and you need to pin memory correctly for cuda graphs.

[04:58] [05:20] Michael: compilation time as in building TensorRT engines?
[05:23] Elena: yes, building engines and kernel selection passes. that can take minutes for large models or if you change max-seq during compile. we provide prebuilt engine variants for common seq lengths to speed deploy.

[05:40] [06:00] Elena: on kernel-selection heuristics: our runtime profiles layer chooses kernels by evaluating three signals: model arch (attn type and head counts), seq-len distribution, and observed memory/latency on sample inputs. we keep a small catalog of kernel candidates and switch when observed perf crosses thresholds.
[06:18] Lina: do you switch online or only during deploy?
[06:21] Elena: we do a hybrid: prefer compile-time selection but allow online switching with constraints. online switching is guarded by a canary policy and rollback if errors or correctness diffs exceed thresholds.

[06:35] [06:50] Samir: question on vLLM - some of our benchs show vllm is better for single-threaded low-batch scenarios. can you explain where each shines?
[06:57] Elena: vLLM's continuous batching is great for high-concurrency low-batch workloads; its scheduler is optimized for CPU/GPU handoff and dynamic batching. TensorRT-LLM's strength is optimized kernels and fusion: for large batches and long sequences it wins. key tradeoffs: latency tail vs avg throughput and contiguity of memory layout.

[07:26] [07:45] Michael: what about memory footprint with kv cache? we need >32k context for some customers.
[07:51] Elena: kv cache grows linearly with seq length and heads; with FP16 it's big and with 4-bit quant it shrinks but you must handle dequantization overhead. we do prefix compression for long-lived sessions and chunked KV flushing for rarely accessed older context. there are tradeoffs on CPU overhead for compress/decompress.

[08:18] [08:40] Jamal: can we avoid re-capture when we get dynamic lengths?
[08:44] Elena: two strategies: 1) conservative capture: capture a superset graph for the max bucket (higher memory but avoids recapture), 2) incremental graph stitching where we capture smaller graphs and chain them. stitching is complicated and not fully stable across every model. we recommend option 1 for low-variance workloads and stitching for very variable workloads if you can tolerate complexity.

[09:10] [09:30] Lina: how do you validate correctness when switching kernels? sometimes outputs diverge slightly with different fused kernels.
[09:36] Elena: we run a per-token diff with thresholds based on logit deltas; we also run evals on small test prompts. if divergence passes threshold we mark the kernel candidate as unsafe. there's also a shadow-run mode to compare latency/outputs before full switch.

[09:55] [10:20] Michael: can we get those eval harnesses? we have a set of in-house prompts for hallucination/regression checks.
[10:25] Samir: yes we'll share our eval harness and you can plug your prompts. elena will attach the regression scripts.

[10:32] [11:00] Elena: moving to quantization - we support 8-bit and two 4-bit modes. 8-bit gives predictable perf improvements and minimal quality loss. 4-bit needs calibration and sometimes small quality regressions on rare tokens. with TRT-LLM quant kernels we saw ~1.8-2.5x throughput improvement but some drop in top-1 accuracy on sensitive prompts.
[11:22] Michael: are you using QAT or PTQ?
[11:25] Elena: mostly PTQ with per-channel calibration; for some customers we do a light QAT pass. QAT can be heavy but helps for high-accuracy needs.

[11:35] [12:00] Jamal: what's the operational burden for quantized engines? more ops complexity?
[12:05] Elena: yes slightly higher. must store multiple engine variants (fp16, int8, 4bit) and have routing logic to pick based on quality/latency needs. also monitoring needs to track quality metrics since regressions can be subtle.

[12:18] [12:40] Samir: let's talk about batching - you mentioned continuous batching and tail latency - what's your recommended policy for a product with 95th p99 SLOs?
[12:48] Elena: for strict tail SLOs we use a small fixed batch floor and a latency-aware dispatcher: if request waits > X ms we flush early to avoid building huge batches. continuous batching helps throughput but hurts p99. we also recommend token-batching for streaming scenarios so you batch tokens across open streams.

[13:15] [13:40] Michael: for chat products we saw token-level batching reduce cost significantly but sometimes increased p99 on cold starts.
[13:46] Elena: yep that's the tradeoff. we mitigate with prefix caching and reserving a small warm pool of GPUs to handle cold starts quickly. dedicated capacity helps because you can keep state warm.

[14:05] [14:30] Jamal: about VPC/on-prem profiling - we'll need to keep traces internal. what's required?
[14:36] Elena: we provide a profiling bundle that runs inside your VPC and outputs sanitized traces you can keep. no data leaves your network. we just need temporary access to run tests or for you to share the resulting graphs. the bundle includes a lightweight APM, CUDA graph dumps, and per-kernel timings.

[15:00] [15:25] Michael: how intrusive is the profiler - does it affect perf?
[15:30] Elena: minimal. the capture has some overhead on cold-starts but steady-state impact is small. for very latency-sensitive tests we can do passive sampling.

[15:45] [16:10] Lina: on security - do you support KMS/HSM for model keys and anonymized traces?
[16:15] Samir: yes, for private we integrate with AWS KMS, Hashicorp Vault, and HSM options. traces can be redacted: we never need raw PII to profile kernels.

[16:30] [16:50] Elena: back to kernel selection: one example we saw - a newer fused attention kernel regressed in tail latency for batch=1, seq=1024 because of a mutex contention in the runtime scheduler. It was subtle - avg throughput improved but p99 got worse. we rolled it back and added a scheduling heuristic to avoid the kernel for single-stream low-batch cases.

[17:12] [17:30] Michael: that's exactly what we saw internally. our average went up but customer complaints spiked.

[17:34] Elena: yeah you have to optimize for the right metric. we keep per-route SLO profiles to tune selection.

[17:45] [18:00] Jamal: curious about memory fragmentation with CUDA graphs and engine caching? we've hit OOMs after rolling deployments.

[18:06] Elena: common cause is leaking temporary buffers when engines are reloaded. we use a lease-based allocator to reclaim on engine swap and recommend rolling restarts with staged draining to avoid OOMs. also preallocating a slab for worst-case graph footprint reduces fragmentation.

[18:30] [18:55] Lina: can you quantify tail latency change when using CUDA graphs? our p99 improved in one test by 30% but in another it regressed.

[18:59] Elena: typically CUDA graphs lower CPU overhead and reduce jitter, so p99 improves for steady workloads. but if graph capture causes stalls (due to re-capture) you see regressions. the metric depends on reuse rate; if reuse < 60% you might not see benefits.

[19:30] [19:55] Michael: any tips for tuning graph reuse?
[19:58] Elena: bucket by common seq-len and prefix lengths, and pin the graph for the most frequent bucket. also use a short-lived warm pool to amortize recapture cost. instrument capture counts and recapture events.

[20:20] [20:45] Samir: let's go through a proposed test plan for orion - elena?
[20:49] Elena: plan: 1) reproduce Orion's perf cliffs in staging with arg-matching prompts, 2) run side-by-side TRT-LLM FP16 vs vLLM FP16 with same model weights, measure tokens/s, p50/p95/p99, memory, and engine build times, 3) run quantized variants (8-bit, 4-bit) and evaluate quality on your eval prompts, 4) capture CUDA graphs and kernel timelines, 5) produce a report and config recommendations.

[21:20] [21:40] Michael: timeline?
[21:42] Elena: we can start tests the week of Mar 2 if we get staging access. two-week run then report.

[21:50] [22:10] Jamal: access - we'll open a bastion and provide an S3 bucket for traces. any special IAM roles needed?
[22:15] Samir: minimal roles: s3 write for artifacts and ec2/gce roles to spin test jobs. we can also run using a dockerized bundle if you prefer not to give cloud perms.

[22:30] [22:55] Lina: about reproducibility: do you version engine builds? we saw different builds on the same commit.

[22:58] Elena: we fingerprint builds and store engine metadata - compiler flags, CUDA version, cuDNN/TensorRT version. we recommend pinning runtime libs across staging and prod.

[23:15] [23:40] Michael: any gotchas with Triton or HF Inference endpoints? we've tried swapping engines and Triton had different memory accounting.

[23:45] Elena: Triton adds an abstraction layer that changes memory behavior; sometimes it double-buffers tensors. HF Inference is simpler but lacks some kernel fusions. we typically see TRT-LLM integrated directly into our runtime with better visibility.

[24:05] [24:30] Samir: questions from orion on canary rollouts for kernel changes?
[24:33] Michael: yes, how do you canary safely?
[24:36] Elena: small percentage traffic split, shadow-run outputs for diff, and automated rollback if accuracy or error rates worsen. also reserve a fallback engine variant to avoid full-blast failures.

[24:55] [25:20] Jamal: about monitoring - what signals should we watch?
[25:24] Elena: per-kernel latency histograms, recapture counts, graph reuse ratio, KV cache hit rate, memory fragmentation, and token-level quality deltas on eval prompts. we can give a dashboard template.

[25:45] [26:10] Lina: does redwood expose per-token tokenization breakdown? sometimes tokenization differences cause perf variance.

[26:14] Elena: yes we capture tokenization timing and have utilities to compare token counts across tokenizers. tokenization differences are often the root cause for small perf deltas.

[26:30] [26:55] Michael: ok let's surface a few specific requests: 1) reproduce our 64->65 cliff, 2) run trt-llm vs vllm with seq up to 32k (?) - we can't do 32k on A100 though, but we want to understand scaling.

[27:05] Samir: for very large contexts we recommend chunking and prefix compression; we can test scaling to 32k with model sharding or offloading, but that changes the architecture.

[27:20] [27:40] Elena: note on 32k: kv cache memory and attention recompute explode quadratically for some attention implementations; use sparse attention or block-sparse where possible. we can test with offload to host memory too but latency will be higher.

[27:50] [28:10] Jamal: what about mixed precision stability across kernels? we got NaNs once after a kernel switch.

[28:15] Elena: NaNs usually come from fused kernels that don't guard against denormals or from quantization dynamic range issues. we instrument to detect and fail fast, and have fallbacks to safer kernels.

[28:40] [29:05] Samir: let's cover billing and cost tradeoffs quickly - does TRT-LLM save on cost per token?

[29:08] Elena: yes generally TRT-LLM improves tokens-per-second so CPU/GPU time per token drops. however engine build and storage cost plus operational complexity mean you might pay more upfront. for variable workloads vLLM's scheduler can be more cost-efficient. dedicated capacity also changes the math because you can keep engines warm.

[29:40] [30:05] Michael: do you have a cost model?

[30:08] Samir: we'll share a simple cost calculator factoring tokens/s, GPU hourly, and warm-pool sizing.

[30:20] [30:45] Elena: last technical note: when doing quant 4-bit we sometimes see hallucination increase on numeric prompts; recommend keeping critical routes on fp16 or 8-bit. also pay attention to batch alignment: misaligned batches can cause suboptimal kernel choice.

[31:05] [31:30] Michael: good, can we get the trial credits for a test run?

[31:33] Samir: yes we'll include trial credits and a small dedicated warm pool for the test.

[31:40] [32:00] Jamal: any specific logs or artifacts you need from our side?

[32:05] Elena: CPU/GPU top, nvidia-smi logs, sample prompts, model weights (or a pinned model reference), and your staging infra specs (instances, CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT versions).

[32:25] [32:50] Lina: we'll redact customer data but can provide synthetic prompts that mimic production distributions.

[32:55] [33:10] Elena: perfect. we'll also provide a sanitized profiling bundle.

[33:20] [33:45] Samir: ok quick recap of action items: samir to send benchmark spreadsheet & pricing, elena to upload traces and scripts, lina to share staging access details and prompts.

[33:58] Michael: timeline recap: start tests week of Mar 2, two-week test, report mid-March.

[34:10] [34:30] Jamal: last question - if we go private on-prem do you support air-gapped deployments for the profiler?

[34:34] Elena: yes. we have an offline bundle and runbooks. you can run everything locally and the artifacts never leave the network. we also support HSM-based key management.

[34:55] [35:20] Michael: any final caveats?

[35:24] Elena: just that kernel-level perf is messy and tuning is iterative. expect a couple rounds of tuning and a canary period.

[35:40] [36:00] Samir: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule.

[36:05] Michael: thanks, talk soon.

[36:10] [36:30] (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains occasional mis-words (vllm vs vLLM, TRT-LLM typed as trt-llm), run-on sentences and filler. Links shared: benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/orion-trt-vllm-2026-02-14.csv), profiling bundle (link: https://redwood.example.com/profiling-bundles/orion-2026-02).
